tip: Unreal present: 'se' plus the imperfect subjunctive ('avessi') with the conditional ('comprerei') for a hypothetical.
For places, 'dove' can act as the relative 'where/in which': 'l'ufficio dove lavoro'.
With time words, 'in cui' means 'when/on which': 'la sera in cui' (informal Italian often uses 'che' instead).
'Che' serves as both subject and object relative and never changes: 'la storia che mi ha raccontato'.
Graduating is reflexive in Italian: 'laurearsi', so 'mi laureerò' = I'll graduate.
Use 'in' with most countries and regions: 'in Grecia', 'in Italia'. Cities instead take 'a'.
Reflexive verbs take 'essere', so the past-perfect is 'mi ero svegliato' with 'ero', and 'svegliato' agrees with the speaker.
After 'quando' about the future, a finished action normally takes the future perfect: 'quando avrò finito' = when I've finished.
'Quello che' (or 'ciò che') means 'what/that which': 'tutto quello che vuole' = all that he wants.
After a preceding direct object pronoun the participle agrees: 'l'' stands for 'la lettera', so 'spedita', feminine.
Past unreal: 'se' plus the pluperfect subjunctive ('avessi saputo') with the past conditional ('sarei venuto').
The future perfect can express a guess about the past: 'avranno già cenato' = they must have already eaten.
In questions the future can signal wondering: 'dove saranno finiti?' = where could they have ended up?
'A casa' means 'at home' with no article: 'rimarrò a casa' = I'll stay home.
'In punto' after a time means 'sharp/on the dot': 'alle dieci in punto' = at ten sharp.
'Chi' here means 'whoever/anyone who' and always takes a singular verb: 'chi studia... ottiene'.
Unlike English, Italian may use the future after 'se' for a real future case: 'se continuerà a piovere'.
'Con i quali' is a formal stand-in for 'con cui', and 'quali' agrees with what it refers to: plural masculine 'colleghi' gives 'i quali'.
Future perfect for past speculation: 'sarà stato un malinteso' = it must have been a misunderstanding.
After 'dopo che' about the future, Italian normally uses the future perfect: 'avrete mangiato' (will have eaten), not the present.
After 'quando' for a finished future action, Italian normally uses the future perfect 'avrò finito', while the main clause 'ti chiamo' stays present.
'Entro' marks a deadline, meaning by or within a time: 'entro domani' = by tomorrow.
'Ciò che' is a more formal version of 'quello che': 'ciò che conta' = what matters.
The passive here uses 'essere' plus a past participle that agrees with the subject: 'lettera' is feminine, so 'spedita'.
After 'quando' about the future, Italian normally uses the future 'chiuderà' (closes), where English keeps the present.
'Imparare' takes 'a' before an infinitive: 'imparato a nuotare' (learned to swim).
Italian says 'sotto la pioggia' (under the rain) where English says in the rain.
'Era strano che' triggers the subjunctive: 'rispondesse' is the imperfect subjunctive of 'rispondere'.
'Va fatto' is literally goes done, and 'andare' plus a past participle means must be done: 'questo lavoro va fatto subito'.
'Se solo' plus the imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish: 'fosse' (were), from 'essere'.
